title: Redwood cost/econ discovery with Ironwood Partners
summary: Discovery focused on per-token unit economics across Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Ironwood outlined budgets (~$60k/mo initial), latency SLOs for customer-facing flows, and data residency concerns. Discussion covered batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization, reserved capacity vs burst, and a benchmarking pilot. Action items: send pricing sheet, proposal for Dedicated reserved pool, run a 2-week benchmark with their 50k prompt set, and share security/compliance docs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Avery Chen (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Redwood CSM), Maya Singh (CTO, Ironwood), Liam O'Connor (Head of ML), Sophie Reyes (Finance), Ethan Walker (Infra)

Summary/Topics (auto): cost per token, batching and cache levers, dedicated reserved pools vs hosted pay-as-you-go, security/SOC2/KMS, pilot/benchmarks

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? We'll keep this focused on cost and unit economics, happy to dive into latency or security after.
[00:15] Maya: Thanks Jordan, I'm Maya, CTO at Ironwood. We're evaluating options for customer-facing summarization and reranking. Main asks are cost predictability and latency under 200ms for single-turn prompts. Sophie is finance so she'll push on budget.
[00:30] Sophie: Hi, Sophie here. Roughly we can commit initially in the $50k-70k per month range, but we need visibility on per-token.
[00:45] Jordan: Great. Avery, want to frame how Redwood approaches pricing and the main levers?
[00:50] Avery: Sure, quick overview. Hosted is pay-as-you-go per-token with volume tiers; Dedicated is reserved capacity with predictable throughput and lower unit cost if you commit; Private on-prem brings more ops but can be priced as a managed subscription. The levers you control are batching policy, KV/prefix caching, sequence lengths, and quantization. Those can change cost per generated token materially.
[01:15] Liam: Can you unpack batch and KV cache? Our typical flow has a short prompt (150 tokens) and then a 250 token model-generated summary. We also do reranking where we score 20 candidates.
[01:30] Avery: Right, so batching improves throughput for many simultaneous short requests — it increases tokens/sec but can add a bit of latency if you wait to fill batches. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching with latency-aware thresholds. KV cache, or prefix caching, stores the key/value cache for repeated prefixes — if you have a lot of similar prompts (like templates), we can serve subsequent requests with fewer compute tokens. That cuts total token compute overhead.
[01:55] Maya: How common is prefix reuse in practice? Our templates change a little, so not exact repeats.
[02:05] Avery: Even fuzzy reuse helps — we do partial prefix hits; the runtime can reuse KV up to the matching prefix length. In trials we've seen 10-30% token savings on templated flows. For reranking, batching the scoring calls (20 candidates) gives big savings.
[02:30] Sophie: For budgeting we need example unit economics. Can you give a sample calculation for our workload?
[02:40] Jordan: We'll do a concrete example. Suppose hosted price is $0.0008 per input+output token at your starting tier — that's illustrative. For a single prompt 150 in + 250 out = 400 tokens => $0.32 per session. At 200k sessions/month that's 80M tokens -> $64k/month. But with batching and caching we can often reduce effective compute by 15-30% and with Dedicated reserved commit you can push unit cost lower, maybe to $0.00045 per token depending on commit and model variant.
[03:20] Liam: That per-token swing is big. How does quantization impact quality? We can't degrade our summaries.
[03:30] Avery: We recommend 8-bit or 4-bit quantization profiles for certain model families. Redwood Optimize provides per-workload recommendations and evaluates regen quality. For most summarization models, we see negligible quality difference at 8-bit; 4-bit sometimes needs validation. We can run side-by-side evals on your prompt set.
[03:55] Ethan: On Dedicated, what's the scaling and burst behavior? We don't want tail latency spikes during peak daytime trading hours.
[04:05] Jordan: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and SLA-backed latency percentiles. You also get burst capacity to handle spikes — you're billed for reserved capacity monthly, and bursts are metered. The recommendation is size reserved pool for baseline traffic and allow limited burst credit for spikes.
[04:30] Maya: We have a hard requirement for data residency — all data must stay in our VPC. Private deployment is attractive for that. How does cost compare?
[04:40] Avery: Private can be more expensive upfront because of ops and infra, but it removes egress/data residency concerns. We can provide a managed Private with a platform fee + infra cost or a self-managed package. Often Dedicated in a customer VPC (if that's an option) hits a middle ground. We'll share a breakdown.
[04:58] Sophie: For the sample calculation, can you include caching savings and reserved discount banding? Finance wants fast comparisons.
[05:10] Jordan: Absolutely — we'll send a model with scenarios (hosted at tiered usage, hosted + caching, dedicated committed levels 3/6/12 months, and private one-time + monthly ops).
[05:25] Liam: Also curious on how latency trades with batching. If we lower batch windows, cost goes up?
[05:35] Avery: Exactly. Smaller batch windows reduce wait time but reduce packing efficiency. Redwood's runtime config lets you choose latency SLOs and optimize for cost under that constraint; we can show you curves for 50ms/100ms/200ms targets.
[05:55] Maya: Any benchmarking customers have done for scoring/reranking workloads?
[06:05] Avery: Yes — we ran a benchmark for a quant hedge fund customer where reranking (batch size 32) dropped cost per candidate by ~4-5x relative to naive single-call scoring, while maintaining 95th percentile latency under target. We'll replicate similar for you.
[06:30] Sophie: On security/compliance, we need SOC2, KMS integration, SSO, and audit logs. Does Redwood provide that for hosted?
[06:40] Jordan: Hosted offers SOC2, customer-controlled KMS for Private/Dedicated, SSO/SAML and RBAC. We will attach SOC2 and network diagrams. For hosted, key management is via Redwood-managed KMS unless you choose Dedicated/Private with customer KMS integration.
[07:00] Ethan: For the pilot, what telemetry do you need from our side?
[07:10] Avery: We'll need your prompt traces (redacted), typical payload sizes, concurrency patterns, and at least a 50k sample prompt set. We'll instrument latency percentiles, token counts, cache hit rates, and cost per token estimates.
[07:30] Maya: That sounds fine. Sophie, is the $60k/mo top-line workable if we see 20-30% savings with dedicated?
[07:40] Sophie: Potentially. We need the math in a spreadsheet. If dedicated brings cost below $0.0005/token at our 80M token runrate, it's probably a go, pending legal.
[07:55] Jordan: Note that reserved commits require a term; we can model 3/6/12 month and show break-even.
[08:05] Liam: One technical detail — your runtime supports KV for long-context? Our templates have variable prefixes up to 1k tokens.
[08:15] Avery: Yes, KV management supports long-prefix caches and incremental KV stitching; the runtime can keep KV shards and reuse across requests where applicable. We'll include more technical docs.
[08:30] Maya: Can we get a POC where Redwood runs our 50k prompts against Hosted vs Dedicated vs quantized variants to show cost/quality/latency?
[08:40] Jordan: Yes — propose a 2-week benchmark: week 1 hosted baseline, week 2 dedicated reserved config + quant profiles and caching settings. We'll capture cost, latency p50/p95/p99, and quality metrics on a holdout set.
[09:00] Sophie: Who owns infra for the Dedicated trial — do we need to provision anything?
[09:10] Jordan: For Dedicated we provision reserved capacity in a region and you point traffic to it. For Private, we coordinate with your infra for VPC peering or on-prem setup. For the trial, we can run a dedicated sandbox in our infra under an NDA, or do a VPC-connected dedicated instance if you prefer.
[09:35] Ethan: For compliance we prefer VPC peering. We'll need a network diagram and port list.
[09:45] Jordan: Noted — we'll send a network diagram and firewall guidance.
[09:55] Maya: Competitors — we've also talked to Anthropic and OpenAI. We're trying to compare unit economics across vendors, especially with large candidate scoring.
[10:05] Jordan: Understood. Redwood's difference is the runtime levers and Dedicated/Private options that make unit costs predictable. We'll include competitor benchmarks where possible.
[10:20] Avery: Technical aside: when scoring many candidates, consider moving scoring models to a smaller quantized model for first-pass, then full model for top-k. That's a common cost-saving pattern.
[10:35] Liam: Good idea — apply cascade scoring. We'll include that in our evaluation.
[10:45] Jordan: To recap next steps: we'll send pricing scenarios and benchmark plan; ironwood shares prompt set; we'll schedule a follow-up to review results.
[10:55] Maya: Sounds good. Any other blockers?
[11:00] Sophie: Legal review timeline is two weeks once we have a procurement sheet.
[11:05] Jordan: We'll aim to get docs over tomorrow. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
